exploratory.title: Information type on sharing vs plausibility
exploratory.rationale: Comparing the effects on the plausibility judgment with those on sharing shows whether the sharing penalty tracks perceived credibility.
exploratory.method: The effect of each headline type against true/neutral headlines was estimated for sharing and for the plausibility choice, using the same specification.
exploratory.finding: Misinformation lowers sharing by 0.182 and plausibility by 0.186; fact-checks lower them by 0.133 and 0.124 (2 arms, 2 outcomes), so the two outcomes move almost identically.

exploratory.title: Information type effect by survey language
exploratory.rationale: The registered effects might differ between English and Spanish respondents, so the pooled estimate is checked in each language.
exploratory.method: The registered information-type effect on sharing was re-estimated separately for English and Spanish survey respondents and compared with the full sample.
exploratory.finding: Misinformation effect is -0.201 (SE 0.014) in English and -0.144 (SE 0.020) in Spanish; fact-check is -0.141 vs -0.119; both arms are negative in both languages, with a smaller penalty in Spanish.

exploratory.title: Information type effect by respondent age
exploratory.rationale: Age was not a planned moderator, and the PAP did not examine whether older respondents penalize false content differently.
exploratory.method: The information-type effects on sharing were compared between respondents above and below the median age using interactions.
exploratory.finding: Older respondents penalize misinformation more (interaction -0.078, SE 0.022), while the fact-check interaction is near zero (0.006, SE 0.023); 2 interactions tested.

lit.text: Prior work bearing on these hypotheses is thin and mostly general. Reviews of misinformation describe its spread and influence as a feature of the post-truth information environment (Lewandowsky et al., 2017). Reviews of conspiracy theories ask which factors are associated with conspiracy beliefs (Douglas et al., 2019), which is relevant to the hypotheses about sharers who believe disputed claims. A cross-national study of COVID-19 misinformation examines predictors of belief in common false statements and links such belief to health behaviours (Roozenbeek et al., 2020). None of these works estimates how sharer attributes such as tie strength, trust, ideology, origin or knowledge affect willingness to share or the perceived plausibility of a post. The retrieved works do not directly disagree with one another or with the study's expectations, because none tests the same source-attribute effects. The nearest tension lies between accounts in which belief in misinformation drives behaviour (Roozenbeek et al., 2020) and the study's interest in sharing without believing (X4), in which sharing and plausibility judgments may come apart. The study's design, with randomized profile features and separate sharing and plausibility outcomes, can speak to that question. It cannot adjudicate the broader accounts of why people hold conspiracy beliefs (Douglas et al., 2019).

sections.abstract: This study asks how the type of information, and who shares it, shape willingness to share a post and judgments of its plausibility. We ran a conjoint experiment with 12,000 profiles from US Latino (Hispanic) adults in a YouGov sample, surveyed in English or Spanish. Only the headline type was randomized; the sharer's tie strength, origin, ideology, trust, knowledge and belief in disputed claims are measured attributes of the respondent's real contacts. Compared with true or neutral headlines, misinformation was chosen 18.2 points less often (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]) and fact-checks 13.3 points less often (95% CI [−15.6, −11.1]). Plausibility showed the same pattern. High trust in the sharer (+5.7 points) and a close tie (+3.0 points) were associated with more sharing. Origin, knowledge and conspiracy belief were not distinguishable from zero. Results come from many uncorrected tests, and the sharer contrasts are descriptive rather than causal.
sections.design_notes: The plan was registered (AsPredicted #132,508). Each respondent chose between profiles, and the outcomes were being chosen to share and being judged more plausible. The headline type was randomized: true or neutral (the reference level), misinformation, or fact-check. The six sharer features describe the respondent's own real contacts, so their effects are descriptive contrasts that bundle correlated attributes. The sample is US Latino (Hispanic) adults from YouGov, surveyed in English or Spanish. All 12,000 raw rows entered analysis, with about 100 dropped from individual models for missing values. The reference group of true or neutral headlines has 4,145 profiles. Standard errors are clustered by respondent.

results.H1: Misinformation was chosen to share 18.2 points less often than true or neutral headlines (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0], two-sided p < 0.001). Fact-checks were also shared less, by 13.3 points (95% CI [−15.6, −11.1], p < 0.001). Baseline sharing for true or neutral headlines was 60.3%. Both are large, and this is the only randomized feature.
results.H2: Close-tie profiles were chosen 3.0 points more often than distant-tie profiles (95% CI [1.0, 5.0], two-sided p = 0.003). This is a measured contrast rather than a randomized effect.
results.H3: Continental US origin differed from foreign origin by 0.2 points (95% CI [−1.4, 1.8], p = 0.81). This is not distinguishable from zero, though the interval rules out large effects.
results.H4: A moderate sharer was chosen 1.9 points less often than a liberal sharer (95% CI [−3.7, −0.1], two-sided p = 0.034), a result near the threshold that should be read cautiously. A conservative sharer was −0.7 points (95% CI [−2.8, 1.5]) relative to a liberal one.
results.H5: High trust in the sharer was associated with 5.7 points more sharing than low trust (95% CI [2.3, 9.1], two-sided p < 0.001). Mid trust was 3.6 points higher, with an interval that includes zero (95% CI [−0.1, 7.3], p = 0.056).
results.H6: Neither mid nor high sharer knowledge was distinguishable from low knowledge. High knowledge was 1.7 points higher (95% CI [−0.5, 3.9]), and mid knowledge was essentially level (95% CI [−2.0, 1.9]).
results.H7: High belief in disputed claims among sharers differed from low belief by −0.2 points (95% CI [−1.9, 1.6], p = 0.87). This is not distinguishable from zero.
results.H8: Misinformation was judged 18.6 points less plausible than true or neutral headlines (95% CI [−20.8, −16.4], two-sided p < 0.001). Fact-checks were 12.4 points lower (95% CI [−14.7, −10.2], p < 0.001).
results.H9: Close ties were associated with 2.8 points higher plausibility (95% CI [0.7, 4.8], two-sided p = 0.008). This is a measured contrast.
results.H10: Sharer origin differed on plausibility by −0.3 points (95% CI [−1.9, 1.4]). This is not distinguishable from zero.
results.H11: A moderate sharer was rated 2.1 points less plausible than a liberal sharer (95% CI [−4.0, −0.3], p = 0.026), close to the threshold. A conservative sharer was −1.9 points (95% CI [−4.1, 0.3]), not distinguishable from zero.
results.H12: Neither mid trust (−0.6 points, 95% CI [−4.2, 3.0]) nor high trust (2.5 points, 95% CI [−0.7, 5.8]) was distinguishable from low trust for plausibility.
results.H13: Sharer knowledge was not distinguishable from zero for plausibility. High knowledge was 1.7 points above low (95% CI [−0.4, 3.8]), and mid knowledge was level.
results.H14: High belief in disputed claims among sharers was associated with a 0.0-point difference in plausibility (95% CI [−1.8, 1.8]). This is not distinguishable from zero.
results.RW: Re-weighting each source attribute by its inverse assignment probability left the picture largely unchanged. The close-tie premium remained 3.0 points for sharing (95% CI [1.0, 5.0]) and high trust rose to 6.7 points (95% CI [3.3, 10.1]). The moderate-sharer effect on sharing weakened to −1.7 points, with an interval that includes zero (95% CI [−3.5, 0.0]). For plausibility, the close tie (+2.7 points) held, and the moderate-sharer estimate stayed significant (−2.1 points, p = 0.030). Other estimates were not distinguishable from zero.
results.S1: Age tertiles differed mainly for misinformation. Respondents in the oldest tertile shared it 6.1 points less often than the youngest (approximate 95% CI [−9.2, −3.0], derived from the SE; p < 0.001). Other feature levels showed no clear age difference. With many subgroup contrasts, treat this as the notable one.
results.S2: Respondent ideology mattered for true or neutral headlines, which the most conservative tertile shared 5.6 points less than the most liberal (p = 0.002). Sharing by a liberal sharer was 4.8 points lower among conservatives (p = 0.017). A few other contrasts were small.
results.S3: Respondents with the most belief in disputed claims shared misinformation 5.6 points more often (p < 0.001) and true or neutral headlines 5.5 points less often (p < 0.001). Several smaller differences appeared, for example for high-trust sharers (−2.3 points).
results.S4: Respondents with the highest media trust shared misinformation 4.8 points more often than those with the lowest (p = 0.003). Smaller differences appeared for sharers with high knowledge and low conspiracy belief; with this many comparisons, they are tentative.
results.S5: Spanish-language respondents shared misinformation 3.6 points more often than English-language respondents (p = 0.010). Differences also appeared for low-trust sharers (+7.9 points) and low-knowledge sharers (+3.2 points), though those are near the threshold.
results.S6: Older respondents rated misinformation 4.0 points less plausible than younger ones (p = 0.013), and liberal sharers 3.7 points more plausible (p = 0.020). Other contrasts were not distinguishable from zero.
results.S7: The most conservative tertile rated true or neutral headlines 4.9 points less plausible than the most liberal (p = 0.006). A smaller difference appeared for continental US sharers (−1.5 points).
results.S8: Respondents with high belief in disputed claims rated misinformation 6.8 points more plausible (p < 0.001) and true or neutral headlines 6.9 points less plausible (p < 0.001). Smaller differences appeared for high-trust and high-knowledge sharers.
results.S9: Respondents with high media trust rated misinformation 4.4 points more plausible (p = 0.007). Sharers with low conspiracy belief were rated 4.4 points more plausible (p = 0.009). Other differences were small or near the threshold.
results.S10: Spanish-language respondents rated misinformation 3.7 points more plausible than English-language respondents (p = 0.008). They also rated low-trust sharers 9.0 points more plausible (p = 0.007) and low-knowledge sharers 3.6 points more plausible (p = 0.016).
results.X1: This is a post hoc estimate. Each additional step of trust in the sharer (1-5) was associated with 1.4 points more sharing (SE 0.4, two-sided p < 0.001).
results.X2: Post hoc. Each step of trust in the sharer was associated with 1.3 points higher plausibility (SE 0.4, p < 0.001).
results.X3: Post hoc. The close-tie premium on sharing was 2.9 points (SE 1.0, p = 0.006), consistent with the registered estimate.
results.X4: Post hoc. Among profiles chosen to share, the share judged less plausible than the alternative was 5.5 points higher for misinformation (95% CI [3.0, 8.1], p < 0.001). Fact-checks were 1.7 points higher (95% CI [−0.5, 4.0]), not distinguishable from zero.
results.X5: Post hoc. Sharing was 4.4 points higher when respondent and sharer leaned the same way than when they leaned opposite ways (95% CI [0.9, 7.9], p = 0.015). Pairs involving a moderate were 0.8 points apart, not distinguishable from zero.
results.X6: Post hoc. Respondents whose networks were seen as more prone to believing disputed claims shared more misinformation (slope 0.110, SE 0.049, p = 0.026). This is a modest, respondent-level association.
results.X7: Post hoc. Congenial content was shared 2.5 points more than uncongenial content (SE 1.9, p = 0.18), which is not distinguishable from zero.
results.X8: Post hoc. The overall slope of sharing on the sharer's perceived belief in disputed claims was 0.5 points (SE 1.4, p = 0.71), not distinguishable from zero.
results.X9: Post hoc. The overall slope of plausibility on the sharer's perceived belief in disputed claims was −0.5 points (SE 1.4, p = 0.72), not distinguishable from zero.
results.X10: Post hoc and thin (266 profiles). The anti-vaccine headline was rated 16.5 points more plausible when the sharer was seen as believing the DNA claim (SE 6.7, p = 0.013).
results.X11: Post hoc. For misinformation, the trust slope on sharing was 1.9 points per step (SE 0.8, p = 0.013) across the pooled health and political headlines.
results.X12: Post hoc. For misinformation, the close-tie premium was 3.5 points (SE 1.7, p = 0.040), near the threshold.
results.X13: Post hoc. The sharer-origin slope on sharing was 0.2 points (SE 0.8, p = 0.78), not distinguishable from zero.
results.XS1: Post hoc. The trust slope on sharing was 1.9 points for misinformation (p = 0.013), 1.7 for fact-checks (p = 0.035) and 0.6 for true or neutral (p = 0.46). The slopes did not differ clearly.
results.XS2: Post hoc. The trust slope on plausibility was about 2 points per step for misinformation and fact-checks (p = 0.009 and 0.023), and near zero for true or neutral headlines.
results.XS3: Post hoc. The close-tie premium on sharing was 4.7 points for fact-checks (p = 0.005), 3.5 for misinformation (p = 0.040) and 0.9 for true or neutral (p = 0.59). The differences between types were not clear.
results.XS5: Post hoc. The congruent-sharer gap was 3.8 to 5.6 points across information types, with intervals including zero in each. No type differed distinguishably from another.
results.XS7: Post hoc. Congenial misinformation was shared 5.4 points more than uncongenial (SE 2.2, p = 0.012). For fact-checks the gap was −0.2 points (p = 0.93). The difference between the two was 5.6 points (p = 0.007).
results.XS8: Post hoc. The slope of sharing on the sharer's perceived conspiracy belief was positive for misinformation (8.6 points, p = 0.002) and not distinguishable from zero for fact-checks or true or neutral headlines. The difference from fact-checks was 13.1 points (p = 0.001).
results.XS9: Post hoc. The slope of plausibility on the sharer's perceived conspiracy belief was positive for misinformation (9.5 points, p < 0.001) and slightly negative for true or neutral headlines (−5.5 points, p = 0.046). The misinformation difference from fact-checks was 14.6 points.
results.XS11: Post hoc. The trust slope on sharing misinformation was 2.5 points for health headlines (p = 0.22; 550 profiles) and 1.9 for political ones (p = 0.024). The difference was not distinguishable from zero.
results.XS12: Post hoc. The close-tie premium on misinformation was 0.7 points for health (p = 0.88) and 3.9 for political headlines (p = 0.031). The difference was not distinguishable from zero.
results.XS13a: Post hoc. The sharer-origin slope was 0.4 points in English and 0.04 points in Spanish. The difference was not distinguishable from zero (p = 0.75).
results.XS13b: Post hoc. The sharer-origin slope was 1.3 points among foreign-born and −0.8 among US-born respondents. The difference was not distinguishable from zero (p = 0.27).

exploratory.E1: Unreviewed code reproduces the registered estimates for both outcomes: misinformation and fact-checks lower sharing and plausibility by similar amounts. It agrees with the registered results.
exploratory.E2: Unreviewed code finds misinformation penalties of −20.1 points in English and −14.4 in Spanish, with fact-check penalties of −14.1 and −11.9. Both are negative in both languages, with smaller penalties in Spanish.
exploratory.E3: Unreviewed code suggests older respondents penalize misinformation more (interaction −7.8 points, 95% CI [−12.2, −3.4]), with no clear fact-check interaction. This is consistent with the registered age pattern.

sections.limitations: Only headline type was randomized, so effects of tie strength, trust, ideology, origin, knowledge and conspiracy belief are descriptive contrasts across respondents' real contacts, bundled with correlated attributes. Nearly eighty tests were run without multiplicity correction, so effects near the threshold, such as the moderate-sharer contrast, deserve caution. Many subgroup contrasts rely on arms of a few hundred profiles, such as low-trust sharers. The post hoc exploratory tests were specified after seeing the data. The sample covers US Latino adults in a YouGov panel and may not generalize to other groups or platforms. Sharing was a forced choice between profiles, not real sharing behavior.

extensions.title: Randomized source cues and separate sharing and belief measures
extensions.why: Fixes the design and measurement causes. Randomizing source cues turns the descriptive trust and tie contrasts into causal effects. Rating sharing and accuracy separately on 1–7 scales lets the two outcomes diverge.

power_target.basis: Observed trust effect of 0.057 (H5) and MDE of 0.051 for Trust: high vs Trust: low. About 1,000 per cell gives an MDE near 0.05 on a 0/1 outcome; closer to 1,300 per cell is needed for the tie effect of 0.03 under clustering.

extensions.rationale: The source study found misinformation lowered sharing by 18.2 points and plausibility by 18.6 points, so the two moved together. High trust (+5.7) and close tie (+3.0) were associated with more sharing, but sharer attributes were not randomized and both outcomes were forced choices. Randomizing source cues and rating sharing and accuracy separately lets the two outcomes diverge.
extensions.contribution: Tests causally whether source trust and tie strength shift sharing intent more than perceived accuracy of a false headline.
extensions.hypothesis: Source trust and tie strength raise sharing intent more than perceived accuracy, especially for the false headline.
extensions.primary_outcome: Sharing intent (1-7) minus perceived accuracy (1-7, standardized), and each rating separately.
extensions.comparison: High vs low trust and close vs distant tie, on sharing versus accuracy, by headline type.

extensions.title: Replication across populations and languages
extensions.why: Fixes the sample cause. The original shows a smaller penalty among Spanish-language respondents (−14.4 vs −20.1), but only within a Latino sample.

power_target.basis: The language gap is 0.057 (−0.201 vs −0.144), with SEs near 0.014–0.020. About 1,500 per group-by-arm cell gives an MDE near 0.04.

extensions.rationale: The source found a misinformation sharing penalty of −18.2 points and a fact-check penalty of −13.3 points, but only among US Latino adults. The penalty looked smaller among Spanish-language respondents (−14.4 vs −20.1), and that gap is confounded with sample. This design runs the same headline-type randomization in white, Black and Latino adults, with Latino adults split by survey language.
extensions.contribution: Tests whether the information-type penalty and the trust gradient generalize across racial/ethnic groups and survey languages.
extensions.hypothesis: The misinformation sharing penalty is negative in all groups, and it is smaller among Spanish-language Latino respondents than among English-language Latino respondents. High sharer trust is associated with more sharing in all groups.
extensions.primary_outcome: Chosen to share (1 if the headline was chosen in 'Which post would you be more likely to share?')
extensions.comparison: Misinformation vs true/neutral headline, with the information-type by group and by language interaction tested. The fact-check vs true/neutral contrast is secondary.
unresolved: The actual headline pairs (17 topics) and their Spanish translations must be supplied by the research team to replace the cond_note text.
Compensation, IRB number and the panel quotas must be set by the research team.

extensions.title: Belief-driven versus identity-driven sharing of misinformation
extensions.why: Fixes the missing_moderator and design causes. Randomizing source ideology and measuring both outcomes lets sharing diverge from belief when sources are co-partisan, which the original could not test.

power_target.basis: Moderator contrasts of about 0.055 (S3) with SEs near 0.017; the sharer ideology effect of 0.019 (H4) is smaller, so a cell of 1,500 targets an interaction MDE near 0.04.

extensions.rationale: The source found misinformation lowered sharing by 18.2 points and plausibility by 18.6 points, so the two moved together. Sharer ideology was not randomized (moderate sharer −1.9 points, p=0.034), and both outcomes were forced choices, so the source could not test whether source ideology pulls sharing away from plausibility. This design randomizes source ideology and measures both outcomes on separate scales.
extensions.contribution: Tests whether source ideology shifts sharing intent more than perceived accuracy, which separates belief-driven from identity-driven sharing.
extensions.hypothesis: If sharing follows belief, the source effect on sharing equals its effect on accuracy. If identity drives sharing, the co-ideological source effect on sharing exceeds its effect on accuracy, especially for false headlines and among respondents in the top tertile of belief in disputed claims.
extensions.primary_outcome: Difference between sharing intent and accuracy rating (both standardized), by source condition, headline veracity and belief tertile.
extensions.comparison: Co-ideological versus opposed and neutral source; outcome (share vs accuracy) by source interaction, moderated by belief tertile and headline veracity.
unresolved: The actual headline texts and outlet names must be supplied and pretested for veracity and topic salience.
IRB approval number and compensation must be supplied by the research team.

results.H11: A moderate sharer lowered plausibility by 2.1 points relative to a liberal sharer (95% CI [−4.0, −0.3], p = 0.026), close to the threshold. A conservative sharer was −1.9 points (95% CI [−4.1, 0.3]), not distinguishable from zero.
results.H12: Neither mid trust (−0.6 points, 95% CI [−4.2, 3.0]) nor high trust (2.5 points, 95% CI [−0.7, 5.8]) was distinguishable from low trust for plausibility.
results.H13: Sharer knowledge was not distinguishable from zero for plausibility. High knowledge was 1.7 points above low (95% CI [−0.4, 3.8]), and mid knowledge was level.
results.H14: High belief in disputed claims among sharers moved plausibility by 0.0 points (95% CI [−1.8, 1.8]). This is not distinguishable from zero.
results.RW: Re-weighting each source attribute by its inverse assignment probability left the picture largely unchanged. The close-tie premium remained 3.0 points for sharing (95% CI [1.0, 5.0]) and high trust rose to 6.7 points (95% CI [3.3, 10.1]). The moderate-sharer effect on sharing weakened to −1.7 points, with an interval that includes zero (95% CI [−3.5, 0.0]). For plausibility, the close tie (+2.7 points) and moderate sharer (−2.1 points) estimates held. Other estimates were not distinguishable from zero.
results.S1: Age tertiles differed mainly for misinformation. Respondents in the oldest tertile shared it 6.1 points less often than the youngest (95% CI roughly [−9.3, −2.9], p < 0.001). Other feature levels showed no clear age difference. With many subgroup contrasts, treat this as the notable one.
results.S2: Respondent ideology mattered for true or neutral headlines, which the most conservative tertile shared 5.6 points less than the most liberal (p = 0.002). Sharing by a liberal sharer was 4.8 points lower among conservatives (p = 0.017). A few other contrasts were small.
results.S3: Respondents with the most belief in disputed claims shared misinformation 5.6 points more often (p < 0.001) and true or neutral headlines 5.5 points less often (p < 0.001). Several smaller differences appeared, for example for high-trust sharers (−2.3 points).
results.S4: Respondents with the highest media trust shared misinformation 4.8 points more often than those with the lowest (p = 0.003). Smaller differences appeared for sharers with high knowledge and low conspiracy belief; with this many comparisons, they are tentative.
results.S5: Spanish-language respondents shared misinformation 3.6 points more often than English-language respondents (p = 0.010). Differences also appeared for low-trust sharers (+7.9 points) and low-knowledge sharers (+3.2 points), though those are near the threshold.
results.S6: Older respondents rated misinformation 4.0 points less plausible than younger ones (p = 0.013), and liberal sharers 3.7 points more plausible (p = 0.020). Other contrasts were not distinguishable from zero.
results.S7: The most conservative tertile rated true or neutral headlines 4.9 points less plausible than the most liberal (p = 0.006). A smaller difference appeared for continental US sharers (−1.5 points).
results.S8: Respondents with high belief in disputed claims rated misinformation 6.8 points more plausible (p < 0.001) and true or neutral headlines 6.9 points less plausible (p < 0.001). Smaller differences appeared for high-trust and high-knowledge sharers.
results.S9: Respondents with high media trust rated misinformation 4.4 points more plausible (p = 0.007). Sharers with low conspiracy belief were rated 4.4 points more plausible (p = 0.009). Other differences were small or near the threshold.
results.S10: Spanish-language respondents rated misinformation 3.7 points more plausible than English-language respondents (p = 0.008). They also rated low-trust sharers 9.0 points more plausible (p = 0.007) and low-knowledge sharers 3.6 points more plausible (p = 0.016).
results.X1: This is a post hoc estimate. Each additional step of trust in the sharer (1-5) raised sharing by 1.4 points (SE 0.4, two-sided p < 0.001).
results.X2: Post hoc. Each step of trust in the sharer raised plausibility by 1.3 points (SE 0.4, p < 0.001).
results.X3: Post hoc. The close-tie premium on sharing was 2.9 points (SE 1.0, p = 0.006), consistent with the registered estimate.
results.X4: Post hoc. Among profiles chosen to share, the share judged less plausible than the alternative was 5.5 points higher for misinformation (95% CI [3.0, 8.1], p < 0.001). Fact-checks were 1.7 points higher (95% CI [−0.5, 4.0]), not distinguishable from zero.
results.X5: Post hoc. Sharing was 4.4 points higher when respondent and sharer leaned the same way than when they leaned opposite ways (95% CI [0.9, 7.9], p = 0.015). Pairs involving a moderate showed no clear difference (0.8 points).
results.X6: Post hoc. Respondents whose networks were seen as more prone to believing disputed claims shared more misinformation (slope 0.110, SE 0.049, p = 0.026). This is a modest, respondent-level association.
results.X7: Post hoc. Congenial content was shared 2.5 points more than uncongenial content (SE 1.9, p = 0.18), which is not distinguishable from zero.
results.X8: Post hoc. The overall slope of sharing on the sharer's perceived belief in disputed claims was 0.5 points (SE 1.4, p = 0.71), not distinguishable from zero.
results.X9: Post hoc. The overall slope of plausibility on the sharer's perceived belief in disputed claims was −0.5 points (SE 1.4, p = 0.72), not distinguishable from zero.
results.X10: Post hoc and thin (266 profiles). The anti-vaccine headline was rated 16.5 points more plausible when the sharer was seen as believing the DNA claim (SE 6.7, p = 0.013).
results.X11: Post hoc. For misinformation, the trust slope on sharing was 1.9 points per step (SE 0.8, p = 0.013) across the pooled health and political headlines.
results.X12: Post hoc. For misinformation, the close-tie premium was 3.5 points (SE 1.7, p = 0.040), near the threshold.
results.X13: Post hoc. The sharer-origin slope on sharing was 0.2 points (SE 0.8, p = 0.78), not distinguishable from zero.
results.XS1: Post hoc. The trust slope on sharing was 1.9 points for misinformation (p = 0.013), 1.7 for fact-checks (p = 0.035) and 0.6 for true or neutral (p = 0.46). The slopes did not differ clearly.
results.XS2: Post hoc. The trust slope on plausibility was about 2 points per step for misinformation and fact-checks (p = 0.009 and 0.023), and near zero for true or neutral headlines.
results.XS3: Post hoc. The close-tie premium on sharing was 4.7 points for fact-checks (p = 0.005), 3.5 for misinformation (p = 0.040) and 0.9 for true or neutral (p = 0.59). The differences between types were not clear.
results.XS5: Post hoc. The congruent-sharer gap was 3.8 to 5.6 points across information types, with intervals including zero in each. No type differed distinguishably from another.
results.XS7: Post hoc. Congenial misinformation was shared 5.4 points more than uncongenial (SE 2.2, p = 0.012). For fact-checks the gap was −0.2 points (p = 0.93). The difference between the two was 5.6 points (p = 0.007).
results.XS8: Post hoc. The slope of sharing on the sharer's perceived conspiracy belief was positive for misinformation (8.6 points, p = 0.002) and not distinguishable from zero for fact-checks or true or neutral headlines. The difference from fact-checks was 13.1 points (p = 0.001).
results.XS9: Post hoc. The slope of plausibility on the sharer's perceived conspiracy belief was positive for misinformation (9.5 points, p < 0.001) and slightly negative for true or neutral headlines (−5.5 points, p = 0.046). The misinformation difference from fact-checks was 14.6 points.
results.XS11: Post hoc. The trust slope on sharing misinformation was 2.5 points for health headlines (p = 0.22; 550 profiles) and 1.9 for political ones (p = 0.024). The difference was not distinguishable from zero.
results.XS12: Post hoc. The close-tie premium on misinformation was 0.7 points for health (p = 0.88) and 3.9 for political headlines (p = 0.031). The difference was not distinguishable from zero.
results.XS13a: Post hoc. The sharer-origin slope was 0.4 points in English and 0.04 points in Spanish. The difference was not distinguishable from zero (p = 0.75).
results.XS13b: Post hoc. The sharer-origin slope was 1.3 points among foreign-born and −0.8 among US-born respondents. The difference was not distinguishable from zero (p = 0.27).

exploratory.E1: Unreviewed code reproduces the registered estimates for both outcomes: misinformation and fact-checks lower sharing and plausibility by similar amounts. It agrees with the registered results.
exploratory.E2: Unreviewed code finds misinformation penalties of −20.1 points in English and −14.4 in Spanish, with fact-check penalties of −14.1 and −11.9. Both are negative in both languages, with smaller penalties in Spanish.
exploratory.E3: Unreviewed code suggests older respondents penalize misinformation more (interaction −7.8 points, 95% CI [−12.2, −3.4]), with no clear fact-check interaction. This is consistent with the registered age pattern.

sections_draft.limitations: Only headline type was randomized, so effects of tie strength, trust, ideology, origin, knowledge and conspiracy belief are descriptive contrasts across respondents' real contacts, bundled with correlated attributes. Nearly eighty tests were run without multiplicity correction, so effects near the threshold, such as the moderate-sharer contrast, deserve caution. Many subgroup contrasts rely on arms of a few hundred profiles, such as low-trust sharers. The post hoc exploratory tests were specified after seeing the data. The sample covers US Latino adults in a YouGov panel and may not generalize to other groups or platforms. Sharing was a forced choice between profiles, not real sharing behavior.

got_right: Randomizing headline type produced large, precise effects: misinformation −18.2 points (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]) and fact-checks −13.3 points on sharing, against a 60.3% baseline for true or neutral headlines. Both are well above the MDE of about 0.031.

The report is candid that the six sharer attributes are measured traits of real contacts, so their contrasts are descriptive rather than causal. It also re-weights by inverse assignment probability, which leaves the close-tie and high-trust results intact (R: +3.0 and +6.7 points).

Collecting both sharing and plausibility for each profile, with a registered plan and registered moderators, allows a direct test of whether the two diverge. The E1 comparison shows they largely do not (−18.2 vs −18.6).

why_it_did_not_land.detail: The sharer features are respondents' own ratings of real contacts, so trust, tie, ideology and knowledge are bundled and confounded. The study cannot say whether source attributes matter causally, which is the 'who shares what from whom' premise in the title.
why_it_did_not_land.evidence: Design section: only information type is randomized. The tie contrast of +3.0 points and the high-trust contrast of +5.7 points are labelled descriptive.

why_it_did_not_land.detail: The low-trust, low-knowledge and foreign-origin reference groups are small, so the null results for the sharer attributes are weakly informative. Even naive MDEs exceed plausible effects, and they ignore clustering.
why_it_did_not_land.evidence: The Trust: low reference has n=828 and an MDE of 0.051–0.056. The observed mid-trust effect of 0.036 has p=0.056. The MDE for origin is 0.032, against an observed 0.002.

why_it_did_not_land.detail: Sharing and plausibility are both forced-choice picks between two profiles. The two outcomes are nearly identical, so the study cannot separate sharing from believing. Sharing is stated, not behavioural.
why_it_did_not_land.evidence: Misinformation effect of −0.182 on sharing vs −0.186 on plausibility. Per-model N is about 11,880.

why_it_did_not_land.detail: Respondents' own belief in disputed claims and their media trust flip the misinformation effect, but sharer attributes do not interact with these moderators. The moderator results are many uncorrected subgroup contrasts, so they are exploratory.
why_it_did_not_land.evidence: S3: highest minus lowest tertile of belief in disputed claims +5.6 points for misinformation (p<0.001) and −5.5 points for true or neutral headlines. S4: +4.8 points for misinformation with high media trust.

why_it_did_not_land.detail: The sample is US Latino YouGov panelists only. The language split shows the misinformation penalty differs (English −20.1 vs Spanish −14.4), so the headline result may not carry to other populations.

debates.label: Is sharing misinformation driven by belief?
debates.position_a: Sharing tracks perceived plausibility, so susceptibility to misinformation is a belief problem and corrections should target accuracy.
debates.position_b: Sharing and belief come apart depending on who the source is and on group or identity motives, so conspiracy-prone sharers or people may spread claims regardless of plausibility.
debates.what_this_study_says: Leans to position A on average, since the share and plausibility effects are nearly identical. Because both outcomes are forced choices and the sharer attributes are not randomized, it cannot test whether source attributes pull sharing away from plausibility. Respondents' belief in disputed claims raises misinformation sharing and plausibility alike (S3 and S8).

briefs.title: Randomized source cues and separate sharing and belief measures
briefs.question: Do randomly assigned source trust and tie strength change willingness to share a false headline more than they change its perceived accuracy?
briefs.why_this_fixes_the_failure: Fixes the design and measurement causes. Randomizing source cues turns the descriptive trust and tie contrasts into causal effects. Rating sharing and accuracy separately on 1–7 scales lets the two outcomes diverge.
briefs.design_sketch: Respondents see a single headline (true, false or fact-check) attributed to a fictional contact, with tie (close or distant) and trust (high or low) randomized, which gives a 3×2×2 factorial. Each respondent rates sharing intent and perceived accuracy on separate scales, and a subsample makes a real, incentivized share-or-not choice. Recruit US Latino YouGov adults, stratified by survey language.

power_target.basis: Observed trust effect of 0.057 (H5) and MDE of 0.051 for Trust: high vs Trust: low. About 1,000 per cell gives an MDE near 0.05 on a 0/1 outcome; closer to 1,300 per cell is needed for the tie effect of 0.03 under clustering.

briefs.title: Belief-driven versus identity-driven sharing of misinformation
briefs.question: Does sharing of a false claim follow its perceived plausibility, or does it vary with source ideology independently of plausibility?
briefs.why_this_fixes_the_failure: Fixes the missing_moderator and design causes. Randomizing source ideology and measuring both outcomes lets sharing diverge from belief when sources are co-partisan, which the original could not test.
briefs.design_sketch: Show a false or true headline from a randomized source (co-ideological, opposed, or neutral) to respondents classified by their own ideology and belief in disputed claims. Measure accuracy judgements and sharing intent on separate scales, and test the interaction of source ideology with outcome in a within-subject design. If sharing follows belief, the source effect on both outcomes is the same; if identity drives sharing, the source effect on sharing exceeds its effect on accuracy.

power_target.basis: Moderator contrasts of about 0.055 (S3) with SEs near 0.017; the sharer ideology effect of 0.019 (H4) is smaller, so a cell of 1,500 targets an interaction MDE near 0.04.

briefs.title: Replication across populations and languages
briefs.question: Does the misinformation sharing penalty and the source-trust gradient hold in non-Latino and in Spanish- versus English-language samples?
briefs.why_this_fixes_the_failure: Fixes the sample cause. The original shows a smaller penalty among Spanish-language respondents (−14.4 vs −20.1), but only within a Latino sample.
briefs.design_sketch: Run the same conjoint with the same randomized headline type on matched YouGov samples of white, Black and Latino adults, with Latino respondents split by survey language. Keep the outcomes and registered moderators unchanged. Test whether the information-type effect varies by group and language.

power_target.basis: The language gap is 0.057 (−0.201 vs −0.144), with SEs near 0.014–0.020. About 1,500 per group-by-arm cell gives an MDE near 0.04.

potential.verdict: A follow-up is worth running. The headline result is solid: misinformation is shared and believed about 18 points less, and the study's main gap is causal inference about sources, since every sharer attribute was measured rather than assigned. Run Randomized source cues and separate sharing and belief measures first. It randomizes trust and tie, which carried the only notable sharer signals (+5.7 and +3.0 points), and it separates sharing from belief, which the forced-choice outcomes here conflate. The belief-versus-identity design comes second and the cross-population replication third.
